text.p: Ameritech Corp expects revenue growth to accelerate once the company enters the lucrative long-distance telephone market, complementing the double-digit growth it has enjoyed in quarterly operating earnings.

"We're on target, on plan and going strong," Oren Schaffer, chief financial officer, said in an interview Tuesday, after the company reported a second quarter operating earnings gain of over 10 percent.
It was the fifteenth consecutive quarter of double-digit earnings growth for the regional Baby Bell.

"On the revenue side, we believe this company is capable of double-digit revenue growth when the markets are opened up and we're allowed into the long-distance business," Schaffer said, adding that in the meantime middle to high single-digit growth is sustainable.

Early Tuesday, Ameritech reported second quarter operating earnings of $624 million, up 10.1 percent from last year's $567 million. Operating earnings per share were $1.13 a share versus $1.02 -- a 10.8 percent jump. According to First Call, the consensus estimate was $1.12 a share and the range was $1.10 to $1.13.
Net income, including a one-time $87 million charge for workforce restructuring at one of its international investments, was $537 million or $0.97 a share.
Revenues climbed to $3.99 billion from $3.74 billion and were on the low side of analysts' expectations.

Schaffer said Ameritech has resubmitted information for its Michigan application to become the first Baby Bell in the long distance market. The Federal Communications Commission is expected to rule on the filing around August 19.

The long-distance market in its five-state region is pegged at $9 billion. Schaffer said Ameritech will likely file to offer long distance in Illinois in upcoming weeks and hopes to apply in its three other states by the end of the year.
Ameritech shares were off 10/16 at 67-11/16 in afternoon composite trading.
Robert Wilkes, an analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman, called the results solid and broadly in line with expectations. "Ameritech certainly didn't have a positive surprise," he said.
Analysts pointed out that the number of telephone lines grew 3.3 percent from last year -- a slight improvement from the 3.2 percent posted in first quarter.

"(The growth) is targeted into areas where we feel not only will we put another unit, i.e. an access line, out there, but also it's going to be in a place where there's a high propensity to consume, so there's better revenue coming out of those access lines," Schaffer said.

Higher revenues, he said, are in areas such as "call management services", like call waiting or caller ID. Sales in this high-margin, largely software-based segment rose 22 percent versus second quarter last year, and Schaffer said the company has a "tremendous growth opportunity" there.

"The strategy is to drive the growth of high-value services that are not as asset-intensive, and they clearly have succeeded in this quarter," said William Vogel, an analyst with Montgomery Securities.
